Auxetic ChessProject record · built 2026-09-17 from feat/phaser

Auxetic Chess

Normal chess with one twist: after every move, all sixteen 2×2 blocks of the board turn a quarter and carry the pieces standing on them, so the position keeps getting scrambled — a4 becomes b4, one cell round the block, pawns included. A pawn only ever moves forward, never sideways or backwards, but the board will carry it anywhere. It is the default game, not an option. The board is also a rotating-squares auxetic mechanism — sixteen rigid tiles, hinged at their corners, that bloom open to exactly twice their area and close into a solid 8×8 to play on. Built after a 3D-printed physical board by Ruven Bals, which Luqman sent over as a video on 2026-09-12; the twist was his own idea, added 2026-09-13.

Why this project exists

Luqman sent a video of a 3D-printed folding chess board and asked for the game. The interesting part is not chess — it is the mechanism. A rotating-squares auxetic lattice has a negative Poisson's ratio: pull it on one axis and it grows on both. Rendering that honestly, from the kinematic constraint rather than a tween, is what makes the piece worth showing.

What counts as "done"

  1. Legal chess, with no exceptions — castling, en passant, promotion, and every draw rule. Verified by perft, not by eye.
  2. The fold is derived from the hinge constraint, so the tiles stay joined at every angle.
  3. An opponent worth playing, and four strengths so it is not only for one level.
  4. Playable on a phone as well as a desktop.
  5. The twist is a real mechanic, not decoration: it lives inside the engine, so the search plays the variant properly, and it can never freeze the game (added 2026-09-13, D-006/D-007).

All five hold as of 2026-09-14.

The twist, in one line

Each block cycles its contents a1→a2→b2→b1 — so a4→b4 — for every piece. It can never capture, nothing leaves or enters a block, four turns is the identity, and the whole thing stands down on any turn where turning would expose the mover's king. A pawn's own moves stay forward-only regardless of where it is carried.

The fold, in one line

For the corner hinges to stay joined, tile pitch is fixed by the rotation: d = a·√2·cos(45° + θ), with tiles alternating +θ / −θ in a checkerboard. θ = 0° is the solid playable board; θ = −45° is fully bloomed at exactly 2× the area.

How the game gets made

Pipeline

Auxetic Chess started as a 21-second video of a 3D-printed board and is built in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no dependencies. Each layer is proved by numbers before the next goes on top: the geometry before any drawing, perft before the search, engine suites before the browser, and a browser suite that clicks the real page before a merge.

  1. The objectLuqman sends a video of Ruven Bals's folding board. Frames are pulled with a small Swift and AVFoundation script to identify it.07-references.md
  2. The forkA printable model or a playable game? He chooses the game.06-decisions.md · D-001
  3. The geometryThe hinge constraint is derived, then checked in plain Node before any rendering code exists.test/geom_check.js
  4. Rules engineA 0x88 board with move generation, SAN and FEN. The twist and the stops run inside make and unmake, so the search plays the variant.js/chess.js
  5. PerftMove generation is counted against 26 published reference numbers, and the plain rules are re-checked with the twist off.test/perft.js
  6. SearchNegamax with alpha-beta, quiescence and killer moves, four strengths, a price on stops, and piece tables averaged over each block's four squares.js/ai.js · test/ai_test.js
  7. Variant suitesNode tests for the twist and for stop turning: the permutation, exact undo, legality against a twist-free clone, the stop rules.test/twist_test.js · test/stop_test.js
  8. Board and piecesCanvas renderer for the fold and the turn, with the tile and the six piece types baked once into offscreen sprites.js/board.js · js/pieces.js
  9. Game wiringInput, the computer's turn, two-player mode, undo, the stop button and the checkmate card.js/main.js · index.html · style.css
  10. Browser suitesA hand-rolled DevTools Protocol client drives headless Chrome and clicks the real page: castling, the twist, hotseat, undo, stops.test/cdp.js · test/run.sh
  11. ScreenshotsThe browser suites save pictures of the states they check. The pictures on this page come from them and from a docs pass.test/shots/ · docs/shots/
  12. Branch and mergeWork goes on a feature branch, is committed and pushed to GitHub, and is merged into main with --no-ff.git · github.com/juslangit/auxetic-chess

Tools

Canvas 2DDraws the board, the fold, the turning blocks and the pieces. Offscreen canvases hold the baked sprites.

What the player sees

Screens

Screenshots from the game. Each carries the date it was taken: older ones show the game as it was then, and are kept as a record rather than replaced.

The board and its fold

The rotating-squares mechanism the game is named after. Tile spacing comes from the hinge constraint d = a·√2·cos(45° + θ), not from an animation curve.

One move, frame by frame

The twist is the whole game: after every move all sixteen 2×2 blocks turn a quarter and carry what stands on them. The first five frames are 1. e4 in two-player mode, with the turn held still for each picture.

Playing a game

Two players on one keyboard, or the computer at four strengths. Each side has three stops, and a stop holds the board still for your move and the reply.

Also fixed on the way in (7d4417a): cleanName's character class held raw 0x00, 0x1f and 0x7f bytes where \x00, \x1f, \x7f were meant. It matched the same characters, so no behaviour was ever wrong, but the NUL made git treat js/leaderboard.js as a binary file — no diffs, no merges — and any tool that strips control characters would have silently rewritten the class as [-\x1f\x7f], which matches something else entirely. js/leaderboard.js is a source for the edge function, so the generated engine.js carried the same bytes and was rebuilt. Two bugs found and fixed on the way, both silent:

  • Phaser.AUTO is refused when Phaser is handed an existing canvas ("Must set explicit renderType in custom environment"), so the renderer is now detected with a throwaway probe canvas and named outright.
  • camera.enableFilters() does not exist — enableFilters is a game-object method, and a camera always has its filter list. The call threw inside a try, so the vignette was simply never applied and nothing said so. Worth remembering: a try/catch around decoration hides the decoration failing.

Also corrected before it shipped: the first attempt used Phaser's zoom for retina sharpness, which does not do that — it scales the canvas's CSS size and leaves the backing store alone, so the board would have rendered at 1x and come out blurrier than the version it replaced.

Next, if it continues
  • Parametric printable version (see D-001) — the geometry is already written.
  • An online leaderboard shared between devices — needs a Supabase project Luqman creates, hosting, and a server-side check on results (D-017).
  • PGN export, so a game can be shared or analysed.
  • Opening book, to stop the Strong level repeating one line.
  • Online play — needs the search moved to a worker first (D-004). That would also let the table keep turning while the engine thinks, instead of the turn having to finish first.
  • If a visually irregular board is wanted, only a subset of blocks can turn (D-008) — a different mechanic, worth its own decision.
  • Twist direction is fixed clockwise; alternating it per move, or per block, would change the character a lot and is cheap to try.

06-decisions.md · 26 sections

Decisions

One decision = one entry. Never delete old entries — mark them Superseded by D-00X.
D-001 — Digital game, not a printable model
  • Date: 2026-09-12
  • Status: active
  • Context: The source video is a physical 3D print. "Make this chess game" could mean model it for the BambuLab or build a playable game. The two share almost no work, so it had to be settled before starting.
  • Options considered:
OptionProsCons
Printable STLsMatches Luqman's hardware and 3D skillHinge tolerances need several test prints; not playable
Digital gamePlayable, shareable, portfolio-readyDoes not use the printer
BothGeometry carries overMuch longer
  • Decision: Digital, playable, in the browser. Luqman chose it directly.
  • Consequence: The parametric tile/hinge model is still unbuilt. If it is wanted later, the geometry in js/board.js is the starting point.
D-002 — Expansion direction, not collapse
  • Date: 2026-09-12
  • Status: active
  • Context: d = a·√2·cos(45°+θ) is valid for θ either side of zero. θ > 0 collapses the board toward a point (how you pack the real one away); θ < 0 blooms it open into a lattice. Only one could be the animation.
  • Decision: Use the expansion direction, θ from −45° to 0.
  • Reasoning: At θ → +45° the pitch goes to zero, so in a flat 2D render the tiles interpenetrate and read as a muddle — the physical board only survives it because tiles stack in the third dimension. The expansion direction has no overlap at any angle, doubles the area, and is the actual auxetic signature worth showing.
  • Consequence: A new game blooms closed into play; the end of a game blooms it back open. A "pack away" animation would need real 3D.
D-003 — One baked tile sprite for all sixteen
  • Date: 2026-09-12
  • Status: active
  • Context: Drawing each tile's checkerboard, bevel and hinge pins live cost 4 fps, because ctx.filter = blur() per tile per frame is ruinous.
  • Decision: Bake the tile body, the hinge pin, the backdrop and every piece into offscreen canvases once, then blit.
  • Reasoning: Every tile carries the same 2×2 patch. A tile starts on an even file and even rank, so its local colour parity is (u+v)%2 whichever tile it is — and that parity is unchanged by flipping the board. One sprite therefore serves all sixteen, in both orientations. This is the same fact that lets the physical board be printed from a single tile model.
  • Consequence: 4 fps → 54 fps under headless software rendering. Only live state (selection, legal dots, check, last move) is painted per frame.
D-004 — Search runs on the main thread, inside a time budget
  • Date: 2026-09-12
  • Status: active
  • Context: A Web Worker would keep the UI responsive while the engine thinks.
  • Decision: No worker. Search synchronously with a per-level time budget (120 ms to 4 s), yielding one frame first so "Thinking…" paints.
  • Reasoning: Chrome blocks blob: workers from a file:// origin, so a worker version would only run from a server. Opening index.html directly had to keep working.
  • Consequence: The tab is blocked for up to ~4 s on the Brutal level. If online play is ever added, revisit this with a proper server-served worker.
D-005 — The table turns a quarter after every move
  • Date: 2026-09-12
  • Status: reversed 2026-09-13 — superseded by D-006. This was a misreading of what Luqman asked for. He wanted a game mechanic that scrambles the position; I built a cosmetic whole-table spin. The code was removed rather than left switched off, so it would not fight the real mechanic. Kept here because the two lessons in it still hold: rotating a playable board means inverting the input, and a transition has to be atomic or input leaks into the pause.
  • Context: Luqman asked for the board to rotate itself 90° once a player finishes a turn, so it comes round to face the other side.
  • Decision: A whole-board rotation applied as a transform on the way to the screen, kept separate from the logical file/rank mapping that flipped uses. On by default, with a Spin table toggle.
  • Reasoning and the three things it forced:
    1. Input has to be un-rotated. A click is mapped back through the inverse rotation before it is read as a square. This is the part that actually breaks, so it is tested at 0/90/180/270° and with the board flipped.
    2. The board must shrink mid-turn. A square of side L rotated by φ has a bounding box of L·(|cos φ| + |sin φ|), 1.41× at 45°. The board is already 0.86 of the stage, so a naive quarter turn throws the corners off screen. Scale backs off by min(1, (0.98/0.86)/(|cos φ|+|sin φ|)) — 1 at every rest position, ~0.81 at the midpoint, peaking at 98% of the stage. It reads as the board lifting slightly as it turns.
    3. The turn must finish before the engine thinks. The search blocks this thread (D-004), so starting it mid-rotation freezes the animation halfway. advanceTurn awaits the spin, then hands over.
  • Pieces do not turn with the board. Five of the six types are lathe shapes and look identical from any direction, so keeping them upright is what actually happens to the real turned pieces when the table spins under them. It also keeps the knight readable, which a 90° roll would not.
  • Consequence: At 90° and 270° the board is side-on, with White's back rank on the left. That is inherent to a quarter turn and is what was asked for; a half turn would be the "face the opponent" version if that is ever wanted.
D-006 — The twist: every 2x2 block turns a quarter, carrying the pieces
  • Date: 2026-09-13
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman, after D-005 went the wrong way: "the game will be play as normal chess gameplay but i want to add a twist to make it interesting by making 2x2 of the square rotate 90 degree after a turn from the player so the chess board will be abnormal ... i want the rotate to be the game mechanics soo it will rotate automatically." Asked which block; answer: all of them.
  • Decision: After every move, all sixteen blocks turn a quarter and carry whatever stands on them. Inside a block the contents go (u,v) -> (v, 1-u), i.e. a1→a2→b2→b1→a1, period 4.
  • Why it runs inside make: because "all blocks" is deterministic, the twist could go in the engine's own make/unmake rather than being layered on top. Move generation, check detection, checkmate and the entire search then see the variant for free, and the AI plays it properly instead of playing normal chess into a scrambling board. This was the single most valuable consequence of the rule being deterministic, and it is why the block choice was worth settling before writing any code.
  • Properties that fall out of it being a permutation of four squares: a twist can never capture; nothing ever leaves its own block; four turns is the identity.
  • Consequences accepted: en passant never arises (a double push cannot be answered once everything has moved); castling rights lapse as soon as a twist carries the king off e1, so castling effectively does not occur; a pawn carried onto the far rank auto-promotes to a queen, with no choice offered because it is nobody's move.
D-007 — The twist yields, not the player
  • Date: 2026-09-13
  • Status: active
  • Context: The first rule tried was the principled one — your move must leave your king safe after the twist — enforced for free by the existing legality test. It deadlocks. The permutation does not depend on what you play, so a king hemmed in by its own pieces is carried onto the same square every time; if that square is covered, every move is illegal. Self-play drew by stalemate on move 3: White's king on e1 always carried to e2, a black queen on d4 always carried to d3, which covers e2. Confirmed by dumping the position rather than assuming it was a bug.
  • Decision: If turning the board would walk the mover's own king onto an attacked square, it does not turn that turn.
  • Reasoning: It keeps normal chess legality exactly — the twist can never take a move away from you, which is asserted directly against a twist-free clone across 160 positions — so the game cannot freeze. It stays deterministic, so it still lives inside make (D-006). And it is one sentence to explain.
  • Measured: it stands down on roughly one turn in seven (24 of 160).
  • Rejected: letting the twist leave your own king attacked and treating it as check would let the opponent capture the king before you could answer; the only fix for that is to make the move illegal, which is what deadlocks.
D-008 — Turning every block cannot make the board look irregular
  • Date: 2026-09-13
  • Status: active — a fact, recorded so it is not rediscovered
  • Context: Luqman's stated goal was "so the chess board will be abnormal".
  • The fact: every 2x2 block of a checkerboard is L D / D L. A quarter turn makes it D L / L D. Turning all sixteen therefore flips all 64 squares and leaves a perfectly regular checkerboard with light and dark swapped — the board's colours alternate each move and never become irregular.
  • Consequence: the disorder is entirely in the piece positions. Worked out before building and reported up front, so the mechanic was not sold on something it cannot do. If a visually irregular board is ever the goal, only a subset of blocks can turn — which is a different mechanic, not a tweak.
D-009 — Pawns are frozen by the twist
  • Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: reversed 2026-09-14 — superseded by D-014. Wrong reading of the rule. Keep the observation that started it (the pawn's move options were already correct; the marker rendered exactly one square above it) — that part still holds and is now asserted permanently.
  • Context: Luqman: "if the player first turn is moving a pawn forward, after the board rotate and the opponent finished their turn, the pawn still can move forward, not left or right or back. fix that"
  • What was actually wrong. The pawn's move options were already correct — traced it: after a push and two twists the pawn on f4 could only play f5, and the move marker rendered directly above it (dx 0, dy −82.9px, exactly one square). What was wrong was the carry: the rotation dragged pawns sideways and backwards. e2→e4 became f4 and then f3 — behind where it started. That is what "left or right or back" was describing.
  • Decision: a pawn is never carried. It holds its square while the rest of the block cycles around it.
  • Why it does not break the mechanic: the pieces cycle among whichever of the four squares are not holding a pawn, in the same cyclic order. Still a bijection, so a twist still cannot capture and never has to resolve a collision. Two pawns in a block → the other two swap; three → nothing moves.
  • A rule it deletes: a frozen pawn can never be carried onto the last rank, so promotion-by-twist cannot happen and that code came out (D-006 had it).
  • Also simpler: the set of pawn-occupied squares is invariant under a twist, so the inverse computes the same free set and undoes it exactly — no need to record the permutation in the undo entry.
  • Consequence: the game plays much more like chess. Pawn structure survives and only the pieces get shuffled. Early on that means the back ranks swap pieces in pairs, since a block of two pawns plus two pieces reduces to a swap.
D-010 — The twist is the game, not a checkbox
  • Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman: "doesnt have to be a check box to make it rotate, it's the default game, it is not a regular chess."
  • Decision: the Twist toggle is gone from the UI and the twist is always on. newGame sets game.twist = true unconditionally.
  • Kept: the engine's twist flag itself, which defaults to off in the constructor. That is what lets the perft suite prove the plain rules engine is untouched, and what the standard-chess rule tests (castling, en passant, promotion) switch off deliberately — en passant cannot arise under the twist, so those cases would be untestable otherwise. It is a test seam, not a player setting.
D-011 — Two-player mode lives in the Opponent select
  • Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: active, except where it lives — superseded by D-018 on 2026-09-15: the Opponent select is gone and Two players is a button on the start screen. The rest (humanPlays, undo by mode, no auto-flip) still holds.
  • Context: Luqman asked for a two-player mode.
  • Decision: hotseat, both sides from one keyboard, added as the first option of the existing Opponent select (Two players, then four computer strengths). Choosing it hides the You play row, since with both sides human there is no colour to pick. Switching between the two modes starts a new game; switching between computer strengths does not, so difficulty can change mid-game.
  • One predicate, not scattered comparisons. Every place that used to ask game.turn === playerColor now asks humanPlays(game.turn). In hotseat that is always true, which is what stops the search ever running: aiTurn bails on humanPlays, so there is no second guard to keep in sync. playerColor survives only to say which way up the board starts.
  • Undo differs by mode, deliberately. Against the computer one undo takes back two plies so it is your turn again; in hotseat one ply is one turn, so it takes back one.
  • No auto-flip between turns. Tempting for hotseat, but the board already turns a quarter every move and spinning it 180° on top of that would be disorienting. Flip stays manual.
  • No new checkbox. Following D-010: the mode belongs in the select that already existed, not in another toggle.
D-012 — The fold slider is gone
  • Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman: "get rid of fold 45 degree slider."
  • Decision: the slider and its wiring are removed. The fold itself stays — the board still blooms open at the start of a game, closes into play, and blooms again when the game ends. What went was the manual control, not the mechanism.
  • Note: THETA_OPEN, animateTo and the whole hinge constraint are still load-bearing for those animations, so geom_check.js still earns its place. The controls panel is down to three rows: Opponent, You play, buttons.
D-013 — Animate each piece to its real destination, not by 90°
  • Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman: "when a piece already move forward and the board rotates, make the piece follow the rotation of the board, in the current game, the piece rotate with the board and then go back to its initial place."
  • The bug, and it was mine. The sweep rotated every piece 90° about its tile centre. That was correct while the twist was a plain quarter turn, and stopped being correct the moment pawns were frozen (D-009): the pieces then cycle among only the free squares, so a destination can be a quarter, a half or three quarters round — and a pawn's is zero. A 90° sweep therefore ended somewhere that was not the piece's square, and it jumped to the right one when the animation finished. On a frozen pawn it was unmistakable: swing out, snap back. Exactly what Luqman described.
  • Decision: sweep each piece by the actual angle from the square it came from to the square it is on. Both are cell centres of the same tile and so the same distance from its centre, which means a pure rotation lands exactly — no fudging, no snap.
  • Direction: always the way the tile turns, by normalising the angle to [0, 2π). A two-cycle between adjacent squares therefore sends one piece a quarter and the other three quarters; they never collide, and both follow the tile.
  • How it was missed: the earlier tests checked board state and paint angle, never where a piece was drawn. The position maths is now its own method, piecePosition(sq, now), and the suite samples it at the start, middle and end of a sweep. That is the test that would have caught this on day one.
D-014 — The carry is uniform: every piece turns one cell, pawns included
  • Date: 2026-09-14
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman: "the pieces should follow the rotation and stay. for example initial pieces location is a4, then the board rotate to the right, the pieces should now be at b4."
  • Decision: back to the plain quarter turn for everything. a4 → b4, a1 → a2 → b2 → b1 → a1, one cell round the block, pawns included.
  • Why D-009 was wrong. Freezing pawns forced the cycle to skip occupied squares, which is what broke his example: a piece on a4 with a pawn on b4 was shunted diagonally to b3 instead of simply turning to b4. The mechanic became hard to predict — the destination depended on which squares in the block happened to hold pawns — and a frozen pawn conspicuously failed to "follow the rotation" at all.
  • His pawn rule still holds, and is the right way round. A pawn only ever moves forward — never sideways, never backwards — wherever the board carries it. That was always true of the engine; it is now asserted for every pawn move in every position across a whole game, so it cannot regress silently. The board carrying a pawn is not the pawn moving.
  • What came back with it: promotion-by-carry (a pawn carried onto the far rank becomes a queen), and the undo record that reverses it.
  • What went away: the free-set machinery, its scratch buffers, and blockBase. Search went from 586k back to 803k nps, since the plain 4-cycle is four writes rather than a scan plus a rotation.
Lesson across D-009 and D-014

Three passes on the same sentence, and the cost each time was interpreting a reported symptom as a specified rule. What settled it was Luqman giving a concrete before/after — a4 then b4 — which is checkable in one line and leaves nothing to read into. Worth asking for that shape of example early when a rule is in doubt, rather than choosing between readings and building.

D-015 — Stop turning: three stops each, covering your move and the reply
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman: "add a button to stop rotate for 1 round ... when white turns to make a move, white can choose to stop the rotate but the effect will on for black too for only that round ... after white turn again, the board rotate normally." Settled with him before building, as concrete move sequences rather than prose (the lesson from D-009/D-014):
    • Length: always two moves — the presser's move and the reply, whoever presses. White: e4 (no turn) ...e5 (no turn) Nf3 (turns); Black: ...e5 (no turn) Nf3 (no turn) ...Nc6 (turns). Chosen over "until the end of the White+Black round", which would give Black's stop one move.
    • Uses: a few per game → 3 each (STOPS_PER_GAME in js/main.js).
    • Who: both sides.
    • Computer: uses stops itself and plans around yours.
  • Added by me, flagged to him: a stop cannot be pressed while one is running (so they never chain), and undo gives a spent stop back.
  • Engine shape: a stop is the move with an F_STOP flag, not a separate action — one move stays one undo record, and search compares "Nf3" with "Nf3 + stop" for free. State is stopsLeft[2] and stopPlies, both saved in the undo record and both part of the repetition key. stopsPerGame defaults to 0 in the engine, like twist, so every older suite is untouched.
  • Search: unused stop valued at 100 cp. (Correction 2026-09-15, D-016: the explanation below is wrong — move-one stops are sound tactics, not an illusion.) At 35 cp it stopped on move one: the piece-square tables are plain chess, so a board that stops turning keeps pieces where they "look" good. Stop moves are generated only in the first 2 plies of search — doubling the whole tree dropped strong from depth 4 to 3; limited to 2 plies it is back to 4. Deeper, a running stop is still played out exactly; only pressing a new one is not considered.
  • Known character: in club self-play the computer still takes its first stop early (ply 2 in 3/3 games). One inspected game was a losing side using stops defensively to keep its exposed king from being carried — legitimate, not a bug. Worth watching in real play.
D-016 — Under the twist, score a piece by the average of its block's four squares
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Context: after the root-window speedup, club reached depth 4 and started spending a stop on move one. I told Luqman this was the plain-chess piece-square tables rewarding a board that stops turning, and offered (A) accept, (B) price stops at 2 pawns, (C) twist-aware tables. He chose C.
  • Decision: when game.twist is on, each piece's table value is the mean over the four squares its block carries it through (PST_ORBIT, built once at load, indexed by 0x88 square). Plain chess keeps PST_PLAIN.
  • Evidence it is better: match, orbit vs plain tables, club level, stops on, colours alternating, varied openings: orbit 12 of 16. Turning the board no longer changes the evaluation (pawnless test position: 823.75 before and after; plain tables 820 → 808).
  • What it did not do — my diagnosis was wrong. Move-one stops remain. With material alone the search still prefers them: 1.Nf3, twist, ...Bc4+ exposes White's king; by depth 6 a plain first move is about −430 and a stop about −190 (stop cost included). The early stop is sound play in this variant. Told Luqman plainly and replaced the test that asserted otherwise with "a stop is never spent when it gains nothing" (kings only).
  • Supersedes the D-015 reasoning that "at 35 cp the PST illusion alone made it stop on move one" — the illusion existed, but it was not why.
D-017 — The leaderboard is saved in the browser, not online
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman asked for a leaderboard per computer level. It could live in this browser (localStorage) or be shared online.
  • Options considered:
OptionProsCons
This device onlyNo setup; stays zero-dependency; still opens from file://Each device has its own board
Online, SupabaseOne board for everyoneLuqman has to create the project (the token can't); needs hosting; scores are easy to fake without a server-side check
  • Decision: this device only. Luqman chose it. Superseded by D-019 on 2026-09-15.
  • Consequence: js/leaderboard.js takes anything shaped like localStorage, so moving to an online store later means swapping what it reads and writes, not the rules. If storage is blocked, scores last for the session.
D-018 — Ranked by wins, and Undo makes a game practice
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Context: what puts a player higher, and what Undo does in a game that counts. Asked before building, with previews.
  • Decision (Luqman's choices):
    • Most wins. Draws and losses are not recorded. Equal wins: whoever reached that count first stays ahead. Names are matched without case.
    • Undo is allowed, but the game becomes practice and its win is not saved. The side panel says so. New game is ranked again. Two-player undo is unaffected.
    • The start screen also picks the colour, has a separate Two players button with no username, shows the chosen level's top ten, and remembers the last name.
  • Follow-on, mine: the Opponent and You play dropdowns left the side panel. Changing level mid-game would have moved a game between tables, so level and colour are chosen only on the start screen; the panel has Menu (with "Back to the game") and Leaderboard instead. ai.think reads settings.level rather than the old dropdown.
  • Also: a win is written at checkmate, not when the card appears 700 ms later, so a quick New game cannot lose it. Undo after a saved win makes the rest of that game practice, so the same mate can't be counted twice.
D-019 — Play anywhere: a public link and one shared leaderboard, not online two-player
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Context: friends want to play from their own devices. Asked whether that means a link plus a shared leaderboard, or live two-player between devices too.
  • Decision: link (GitHub Pages) + shared leaderboard (Supabase). Two players stays on one device. Luqman chose it.
  • Stack: a new Supabase project "Auxetic Chess", separate from Sky AI Brain, so no game key is ever near the memory database. The page stays zero-dependency: it talks to Supabase with plain fetch, no supabase-js.
  • The publishable key sits in js/config.js in a public repo, deliberately. It can only read standings; row level security closes the other tables and the database functions are granted to service_role only. Same recorded exception as bluff-show's D-002.
D-020 — Names are claimed with a 4-digit PIN
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Options: free names (anyone can post as anyone), name + PIN, Google sign-in. Luqman chose name + PIN.
  • Details: the first PIN used claims the name (case-insensitive). PINs are bcrypt-hashed in the database (crypt/gen_salt('bf')). Five wrong PINs lock the name for 15 minutes, which puts the 10,000 combinations out of reach. The PIN is checked when Start is pressed, so a typo is found before a win rather than after. The page keeps the PIN in memory for the visit only; the name is remembered in the browser, the PIN never is.
D-021 — The server replays every claimed win
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Options: basic (insert-only table, rate limit) or replay on the server. Luqman chose replay.
  • How: the page sends the move list as short strings (e2e4, e7e8q, g1f3s for a stop). The edge function replays it from the start with the twist and 3 stops each, using server/replay.js bundled with the real js/chess.js by tools/build_function.js — one engine, not a copy. Saved only if it ends in checkmate by the claiming side, with nothing played after the result.
  • Same game counts once per player per level (unique on a hash of the moves), because Strong and Brutal answer identically and a memorised win could be replayed forever. Added by me; told Luqman.
  • Known limit, told to Luqman: it cannot prove the computer's moves were the computer's — someone could play both sides. Nor which level was really played.
D-022 — Start fresh online; offline still plays, unranked
  • Date: 2026-09-15
  • Status: active
  • Decision (Luqman's choice): old per-device wins are not migrated — they cannot be verified. If the leaderboard can't be reached at Start the game starts unranked; if it drops at the moment of a win, the card says the win was not saved. Nothing is queued for later.
D-023 — Publish the link before the shared leaderboard is connected
  • Date: 2026-09-16
  • Status: active
  • Decision (Luqman's choice): put the game on GitHub Pages now and let the leaderboard connect later, rather than holding the public link back until the Supabase project exists.
  • Why: the two are independent. js/config.js ships empty, and with it empty the game plays exactly as it always did — it simply says "Not connected — you can still play, but wins won't be saved" on the start screen and "Not ranked" on the game card. The shared board needs a Supabase project only Luqman can create, and the alternative was leaving a finished game unplayable by his friends while waiting on a two-minute task.
  • What it costs: the first people to play get no shared standings, and their early wins are not backfilled when the leaderboard does come up — consistent with D-022, which already refuses to migrate unverifiable wins.
  • To finish it: create the Supabase project, run tools/deploy_online.sh, run node test/online_live.js, then commit the filled-in js/config.js. The page starts reporting "Online" on the next load. No rebuild, no redeploy of the game itself.
D-024 — Phaser draws the board, and the zero-dependency rule is dropped
  • Date: 2026-09-17
  • Status: active
  • Context: Luqman asked for his web games to be rebuilt on Phaser so they "look, feel and be better at everything". Auxetic Chess went first, as a pilot: it was already a canvas game, so it stood to gain the most and risked the least. The cost is that this project's stated stance -- "no npm packages, no CDN scripts, no fonts fetched" (05-relations) -- is no longer true.
  • Options considered:
OptionProsCons
Keep Canvas 2D, hand-roll the effectsDependency stays at zeroParticles, filters, camera shake and a sound manager are weeks of work each, and worse than Phaser's
Phaser from a CDNNothing in the repoBreaks file://, breaks offline play, and adds a third party who can change or lose the file
Phaser 4.2.1, vendored in vendor/All of the above, still no build step, still works offline and from file://1.4 MB in the repo; the zero-dependency claim goes
  • Decision: Vendor Phaser 4.2.1 and rewrite js/board.js as a Phaser scene.
  • Reasoning: The dependency rule was never the point of this project -- the mechanism was. What the rule actually protected was that the page opens from a folder, with no build and no network, and vendoring keeps every part of that. 1.4 MB buys a WebGL renderer, a particle system, per-object filters, camera shake and a sound manager that can overlap samples.
  • Consequence: BoardView keeps exactly the public API main.js and the six browser tests already used, so the engine, the twist, the leaderboard and all 213 checks were untouched and still pass. Renderer type must be passed explicitly because Phaser is handed the existing #board canvas, and Phaser.AUTO is refused in that case. A WebGL-less browser falls back to Canvas and quietly loses the vignette and the marker glow, which are filters.
D-025 — Sound comes from CC0 samples, not oscillators
  • Date: 2026-09-17
  • Status: active
  • Supersedes: the WebAudio synth described in 00-overview's "State of play".
  • Context: The game's four sounds were oscillators built at runtime, which never had to be loaded but always sounded like oscillators. Luqman named sound as one of four things he wanted better.
  • Decision: Nine samples from Kenney's CC0 "Interface Sounds" and "Impact Sounds" packs, embedded in js/sounds.js as base64 data URIs and played through Phaser's sound manager.
  • Reasoning: CC0 is public domain -- no attribution required, safe to sell, no licence to track (the standing rule for game audio). They are embedded rather than kept as files because Chrome refuses to fetch audio over file://, which would have broken opening the page from the folder, the same constraint that rules out a Web Worker (D-004). Phaser's manager lets them overlap and be pitched, so the piece-down sound varies across a game.
  • Consequence: js/sounds.js is a generated 118 KB file; regenerate it with tools/build_sounds.py, which is also where the nine picks are chosen from the 230 sounds in the two packs.

04-methods.md · 24 sections

Methods

Verify a mechanism numerically before drawing it

The rotating-squares constraint was derived, then checked in plain Node before any rendering code existed: for every θ, assert that the nearest corner of each neighbouring tile pair coincides. test/geom_check.js reports a worst-case gap of ~1e-15 of the tile edge, and the same assertion runs again in the browser against real screen coordinates (~1e-13 px).

This is worth repeating for anything kinematic. A fold that looks right at the two end states is usually wrong in between, and a numeric assertion catches it in seconds instead of after the art is finished.

Perft is non-negotiable for a chess engine

test/perft.js counts leaf nodes against the six published reference positions (start position to depth 5 = 4,865,609; Kiwipete; positions 3–6). All 26 counts match. These positions exist specifically to catch en-passant legality, castling through check, pinned pieces, discovered checks and promotion — the bugs that otherwise surface as a wrong move six months later.

Let the test derive the answer, not the author

The first tactics suite failed three cases, and all three were bad test positions — one asked for Qxh4 from d1, which is not a queen move. Rewritten so the test finds every mating move using the already-perft-proven generator and only then asks the search to find one. A test that encodes my own analysis tests my analysis.

source-atop is canvas-wide, not shape-wide

Shading a canvas shape with globalCompositeOperation = 'source-atop' composites against everything already on that canvas, so a highlight gradient meant for one piece smeared bright columns across the whole board. The fix is also the fast path: draw the shape into its own offscreen canvas, where the only destination pixels are the shape itself, then blit. Same for ctx.filter = 'blur()' — bake it once into a sprite rather than running it per frame.

Walk a lathe profile in one direction

Building a symmetric silhouette by mirroring a profile: go up one flank, across the top, down the other, and let closePath lay the base. Traversing the profile in the wrong order self-intersects the path, and the stroke then draws a spurious diagonal across the piece — a subtle artifact that survived several looks because the fill still came out roughly right.

Drive the real UI with CDP, no dependencies

test/cdp.js is a ~90-line Chrome DevTools Protocol client built on Node's built-in WebSocket (Node 26). It launches headless Chrome, evaluates JS in the page, dispatches real mouse clicks at computed square centres, and captures screenshots. That is what let the browser suite test castling, promotion, en passant, undo and checkmate through actual clicks, and what let the artwork be inspected rather than assumed.

./test/run.sh          # geometry, perft, search, then the browser suite
Guard deferred work with an epoch counter

The AI turn and the end-of-game bloom are both scheduled with setTimeout. A timer from a finished game fired into a freshly set-up one and moved for the player. Every deferred action now captures a module-level epoch that a new game increments, and bails if it no longer matches.

Rotating a board means rotating the input, and shrinking it

Two things bite when you spin a playable board:

  1. The inverse transform. Screen coordinates have to go back through the rotation before they mean anything. Keep the rotation as a transform on the way out (applySpin) and invert it on the way in (applySpin(..., -1)), rather than folding quarter turns into the file/rank mapping — the mapping already carries flipped, and stacking the two is where bugs live. Test the inverse at every quarter and with the flip on.
  2. The bounding box grows. A square of side L at angle φ needs L·(|cos φ| + |sin φ|), so 1.41× at 45°. Anything already filling most of its frame will clip mid-turn. Scaling by min(1, margin/(|cos φ|+|sin φ|)) costs nothing at the rest positions and reads as a deliberate lift.
Make a transition atomic, or input leaks into the gap

The turn was first written as sleep(190) and then start the rotation, so the piece could land before the table moved. For those 190 ms the board looked completely settled — flat, no tween — and the interaction gate re-opened. The fix was to create the tween immediately with a start delay baked into its t0, and clamp t low as well as high in the loop. The gate is false for the whole transition, and the pause still happens.

The test suite found this, twice, before a person could: both a player-side and an AI-side settle() returned early in exactly that window.

An unbounded search extension is a latent crash

negamax had the standard if (inCheck) depth++ check extension. In plain chess it terminates by itself — you cannot stay in check indefinitely. Under the twist you can: kings are carried around every move, so check recurs, the extension fires at every level, depth never falls, and the search runs until the stack dies. The bug was always there; the variant just made it reachable.

Any extension needs a ceiling that does not depend on the rules being searched: an absolute ply cap that returns an evaluation, a cap on quiescence depth, and extensions allowed only so far past the current root depth.

Decide legality by what keeps the game playable, then measure it

Two rules were available for a forced board mutation:

  1. your move must leave your king safe after it, or
  2. the mutation stands down when it would expose your king.

(1) is more principled and came free with the existing legality test — and it deadlocked, drawing by stalemate on move 3. (2) keeps normal chess legality exactly, which is a property worth asserting directly: compare legalMoves() against a clone with the variant off, across a whole game. If they ever differ, the mechanic can take moves away from the player, and a freeze is possible.

Runtime.evaluate awaits promises, so void the ones you are timing

s.eval uses awaitPromise: true. An animation method that resolves on completion will therefore block the evaluate call for the full duration, and every screenshot afterwards lands after the animation finished — which is exactly what made a "mid-twist" capture come back showing a settled board. void view.twistOnce(...) returns undefined, so the call returns immediately and the capture is genuinely mid-flight. Assert the phase you think you caught (alpha between 5 and 85 degrees) rather than trusting the timing.

Separate what turns from what does not

The tile carries the printed checkerboard, so it turns with the twist. The square markers — selection, last move, check, legal-move dots — belong to board positions, which do not turn. Drawing both in one transform is wrong, and at rest it is invisible, because the two differ by a multiple of 90° and the cells line up either way. It only shows mid-animation. Two transforms: paintRot for the tile body, gridRot for anything that means "this square".

Likewise, pieces are positioned by the square they came from during a twist — make has already moved them on — and swung about the tile centre. At a quarter turn the arc lands exactly on the new square, which is worth deriving rather than tuning: rotating the local offset (u-0.5, 0.5-v) by +90° gives (v-0.5, u-0.5), the offset of (v, 1-u), for the flipped board as well as the unflipped one.

A test harness that spawns a browser must also reap it

test/cdp.js spawned a headless Chrome on every run and never closed it. After a dozen runs the orphans wedged the debugging port and the browser suite hung for minutes with no output — which looks exactly like a slow test, not a leak.

Three fixes, all cheap and all worth doing from the start:

  • launch() probes the port first and reuses a live browser instead of spawning a second one.
  • each Session remembers its target id and closes its own tab on the way out.
  • run.sh reaps the browser after the suite (pkill -f remote-debugging-port=...).

The general point: any harness that starts an external process needs the teardown written at the same time as the startup, because the failure mode is silent accumulation and the symptom shows up somewhere unrelated.

Headless Chrome will happily test code you edited minutes ago

The browser suite reported a pawn being carried that the engine demonstrably did not carry — the same scenario passed in node and failed in the browser. The browser was running cached JavaScript. Making launch() reuse a long-lived browser (to stop leaking one per run) turned this from occasional into near-certain.

The fix belongs in the harness, not the tests: create the target on about:blank, send Network.enable and Network.setCacheDisabled, and only then Page.navigate to the real URL. Navigating first and disabling the cache afterwards is too late — the page and its scripts are already fetched.

The tell was a node test and a browser test disagreeing about the same deterministic function. When that happens, suspect the harness before the code.

Trace the thing the user described before changing the rule

Luqman reported a pawn moving "left or right or back". Two readings: its move options were wrong, or the board was carrying it. Rather than guess — having already misread him once — I traced his exact sequence and printed, per ply, where the pawn stood, which directions it could move, and where the rotation put it. That showed move options were already forward-only and the carry was the culprit, which is a one-line description of a real fix instead of a rewrite of the wrong half.

The same trace also caught three bad assertions of my own in a row: a pawn can legitimately change square by being played, by being captured, and its path can legitimately be blocked. An invariant about "nothing else may move it" has to exempt all three, or it fails for the right reasons and looks like a bug.

A [hidden] attribute loses to any class that sets display

Hiding a control row with el.hidden = true did nothing: the user agent's [hidden] { display: none } is beaten on specificity by .row { display: flex }. It needs an explicit .row[hidden] { display: none; }.

Assert the computed style rather than the attribute in the test — hidden === true passes happily while the element is still on screen, which is exactly the bug the test exists to catch.

Replace a scattered comparison with one predicate

Two-player mode touched nine places that all asked game.turn === playerColor in slightly different ways. Rather than add a mode check beside each one, they all became humanPlays(game.turn). The search then cannot run in hotseat for a structural reason — aiTurn bails on the same predicate — instead of because a second guard was remembered in every branch.

"Did it last long enough" is the wrong proxy for "is it playable"

The self-play test asserted plies > 20 to mean the game had not deadlocked. It then failed on a perfectly good 12-ply checkmate. The property actually worth holding is that games reach a legitimate result and that none dies in an early draw — which is the failure the mechanic could genuinely cause. Rewritten to run three games and report each outcome: checkmate@57, checkmate@52, checkmate@35.

Animation correctness needs a testable position function

The twist animation was wrong for weeks-worth of changes and every test passed, because the tests checked board state and the paint angle but never where a piece was drawn. A rendering bug hides from assertions about data.

The fix was to pull the maths out of the draw loop into piecePosition(sq, now) and assert on it directly: at the start of a sweep every piece must sit on the square it came from, at the end on the square it is on, and a frozen piece must not move at any sampled point. Those three checks are cheap, need no pixels, and catch the whole class — including "it looks fine then snaps at the end", which is invisible in a screenshot and obvious in a game.

When an invariant changes, re-derive everything that assumed it

The 90° sweep was correct when the twist was a plain quarter turn. Freezing pawns silently invalidated it, because the permutation stopped being a rotation. The constant 90° was the assumption, written down nowhere. Freezing was later reversed, so 90° is right again — but the code now derives the angle from the two squares, which is what makes it survive the next change to the rule.

Compute a quantity from the things it actually relates rather than hard-coding the value it happens to take. It costs a line and removes a whole class of silent breakage.

Ask for a before/after, not a better description

Three passes were spent on one rule about pawns and rotation, and every pass made the same mistake: reading a reported symptom as a specified rule. "the pawn still can move forward, not left or right or back" can mean the pawn's move options or the board dragging it, and I picked wrong twice.

What settled it in one line was a concrete before/after: a4 → b4. That is checkable, has no interpretation in it, and became a test the same minute. When a rule is genuinely ambiguous, asking for one example of the state before and the state after beats any amount of further prose — including from me.

The project record: docs/index.html (2026-09-15)

One HTML file holds the whole record of the game — overview, pipeline, captioned screenshots, idea, planning, milestones, decisions, methods, session logs, test files and git history — in the repo and on the documentation website. Luqman's standing rule: whenever the game changes, rebuild it and republish, the same as Referee For Fun.

python3 tools/docs/build_docs.py --publish

which rebuilds docs/index.html and then runs docs-site publish, putting it live at https://luqman-docs.netlify.app/auxetic-chess/ — the same link every time. These notes are read directly, so writing the knowledge base is most of updating the record. New screenshots need an entry in GALLERIES at the top of the script; a missing file shows as a labelled gap, not an error. Everything below the script's "engine" line is identical in all four game copies (auxetic-chess, bluff-show, kedai-runtuh, scribble-relay) — change it in all of them at once.

A test that plays chance or races the clock needs both pinned (2026-09-15)

Three engine checks failed a few percent of the time and passed on rerun. None was a game bug. Two things made results differ between runs: random choices (random games, and the engine's own random pick among near-best moves), and a search that deepens until a time budget runs out, so a busy machine searches less deeply and picks another move.

test/repeatable.js pins both without touching the engine: seed(n) replaces Math.random with a seeded generator, and fullDepth(fn) freezes Date.now so a search always completes its level's depth. It works because the engine files are loaded with new Function, which shares the test process's Math and Date.

Two rules that came out of it:

  • Pin the clock only where a test checks which move is chosen. A test that is about speed should measure something the machine cannot change — the "stops don't cost a ply" check now compares node counts, not depth reached in a time limit.
  • Prove the seed isn't lucky. A fixed seed makes a test repeatable, not correct. TEST_SEED lets the suite be swept across many seeds under load; 40 seeds each passed before this was committed.

Measure the flake rate before fixing it, too: the sweep that was meant to reproduce the two known failures found a third.

07-references.md · 4 sections

References

The original object
  • Auxetic Chess by Ruven Bals — a 3D-printed folding chess board. Seen via a repost by viper_chess on Instagram, captioned "Auxetic Chess", sent by Luqman on 2026-09-12. Sixteen tiles, corner pin-and-loop hinges, low wide-based pieces that sit in the tile recesses so they survive the fold. Credited in the page footer and the README.
The mechanism
  • Rotating squares / rotating rigid units — the standard auxetic mechanism. Rigid squares hinged at shared corners; alternating ±θ rotation gives a negative Poisson's ratio. Search terms: "rotating squares auxetic", "rotating rigid units", "negative Poisson's ratio metamaterial".
  • Constraint used here: d = a·√2·cos(45° + θ), derived and then verified numerically in test/geom_check.js.
Chess engine correctness
  • Perft reference counts — Chess Programming Wiki, "Perft Results". The six standard positions and their published node counts per depth are hard-coded in test/perft.js. Start position depth 5 = 4,865,609. These are the numbers to check against if the move generator is ever touched.
  • Kiwipete: r3k2r/p1ppqpb1/bn2pnp1/3PN3/1p2P3/2N2Q1p/PPPBBPPP/R3K2R w KQkq - 0 1
Technique
  • MVV-LVA move ordering, killer moves, quiescence search, tapered piece-square tables — all standard Chess Programming Wiki material.
  • Chrome DevTools Protocol: http://127.0.0.1:<port>/json/version and /json/new?<url> to open a target, then Runtime.evaluate, Input.dispatchMouseEvent, Page.captureScreenshot. Node 26 has a built-in WebSocket, so no npm client is needed — see test/cdp.js.

2026-09-17

What was done

Luqman asked whether Phaser could be used, then asked for all his web games to be rebuilt on it so they "look, feel and be better at everything". Three of his projects are actual browser games: auxetic-chess, scribble-relay and bluff-show.

Before touching anything, the fit was checked and the finding put to him: Phaser is excellent at sprites, tweens, particles and sound, and poor at exactly the two things the other two games are built on — text input (bluff-show is nothing but typing fake answers and picking from lists) and freehand drawing with a finger or stylus (scribble-relay, where Phaser's input pipeline would add lag a drawing app cannot afford). A full rewrite would have improved one game and made two worse, and would have thrown away their 120 and 582 passing browser checks.

Given the choice he took the pilot: auxetic-chess only, on a branch, with the other two untouched until he has played it. He asked for all four of juice, visual quality, sound and phone feel.

  • js/board.js is now a Phaser scene. Phaser 4.2.1, vendored at vendor/phaser.min.js — no npm, no CDN, no build step, still opens from file://. Tiles, pins, pieces, backdrop and markers are game objects instead of drawImage calls.
  • Nothing else was rewritten. The rules engine, the search, the twist, the leaderboard and the six browser suites were not touched. This worked because BoardView already had a clean public API that main.js and every browser test spoke to, so only the inside of the class changed.
  • Sound replaced — nine Kenney CC0 samples, pitch-varied through Phaser's sound manager, in place of four WebAudio oscillators (D-025).
  • Juice added — vignette, a glow on the move markers, a particle burst when a piece is taken, camera shake on check and on mate, a landing bounce as a piece is set down, and a shared pulse so the selected square, its dots and a king in check all breathe on one rhythm.
  • Sharper on a phone, and a ResizeObserver on the canvas so rotating a phone or a growing move list re-lays the board. The old code watched only the window.
  • 213 checks green, no console errors. 52 fps during the fold, against 54 fps for the renderer it replaced.

Decisions made

  • D-024 — Phaser draws the board, and this project's zero-dependency rule is dropped. What the rule actually protected — opens from a folder, no build, no network — is kept by vendoring rather than using a CDN.
  • D-025 — sound comes from CC0 samples, not oscillators.

Stuck on / problems

Three things went wrong, and all three were silent rather than loud:

  • Phaser.AUTO is refused when Phaser is handed an existing canvas. Phaser throws "Must set explicit renderType in custom environment". The existing #board element had to stay — it is what the CSS sizes and what every browser test measures with getBoundingClientRect() — so the renderer is now chosen by probing a throwaway canvas for WebGL and named outright.
  • camera.enableFilters() does not exist. enableFilters is a game-object method; a camera always has its filter list. The call threw inside a try/catch meant to keep decoration from killing the board, so the vignette was simply never applied and nothing reported it. The lesson generalises: a try/catch around decoration hides the decoration failing, so the effect has to be verified as applied, not assumed. Here that meant asserting filters.internal.list.length from the test harness.
  • Phaser's zoom does not make anything sharper. It scales the canvas's CSS size and explicitly leaves the backing store alone. The first attempt used it for retina rendering, which would have shipped a board rendered at 1x — blurrier than the Canvas 2D version it replaced, while claiming to look better. The fix: size the game in device pixels and zoom the camera back by the same factor, scrolling by c*(1-z)/z so world (0,0) lands on the canvas corner. Verified exactly: a 998 px canvas has a 1996×1542 backing store, and world (0,0)→(998,771).

One test failure was not a real one. fold animation runs smoothly reported 2 fps — because a software-WebGL Chrome left running from an earlier experiment was being reused by the harness, and swiftshader at 3 MP is that slow. In the suite's own browser it is 52 fps. The same leftover browser also explains a one-off "console errors" line in a full run that did not reproduce.

Stuck on / problems

  • The fps test failed, and it was my fault. fold animation runs smoothly wants ≥ 50 fps and gave 46, 36, 32, 26, 26 across five runs. I had started a shell busy-wait loop (until [ load < 2 ]; do :; done) to wait for the machine to quiet down — which pinned a core and made the thing I was measuring worse. Killed it, let the load fall, then measured both branches interleaved: main 52/52/54, the branch 52/53/50. No regression. Lesson: never busy-wait for load to drop; and when a timing test fails, measure the baseline before believing the diff caused it. The 50 fps threshold is tight enough to flake on a loaded machine — the same family as the failures fixed on fix/flaky-tests, but not fixed here because it was not what was asked.
  • A NUL byte had been committed. git diff reported js/leaderboard.js as Bin 2874 -> 3799 bytes — git had classified a JavaScript file as binary. The cause: cleanName's character class held raw 0x00, 0x1f and 0x7f bytes where \x00, \x1f and \x7f were intended. It matched the same characters, so the name cleaning was never wrong and every test passed, which is exactly why it survived. It cost diffs and merges on that file, and any editor or pipe that drops control characters would have silently rewritten the class as [-\x1f\x7f] — a different regex. Fixed by escaping all three.
    • My first attempt only escaped the NUL, because I had only counted NULs; the file was still binary and the line then read [\x00-], which was worse. Reverted and enumerated every control byte before fixing.
    • js/leaderboard.js is one of tools/build_function.js's sources, so the deployed edge function's engine.js carried the same bytes; rebuilt.
    • Scanned every tracked file: no others.

What was learned

  • A test suite passing is not evidence that a file is well-formed. This defect was invisible to 213 checks and visible in one line of git diff --stat.
  • Publishing and connecting the backend are separable, and separating them got a finished game into his friends' hands without waiting on a task only he can do.

2026-09-14

Two instructions

Luqman: "get rid of the unnecessary things... doesnt have to be a check box to make it rotate, it's the default game, it is not a regular chess." And: a pawn pushed forward must still move forward after the twists — "not left or right or back."

The checkbox

Gone. newGame sets game.twist = true unconditionally (D-010). The engine's own twist flag stays, defaulting off, purely as a test seam: it is what lets perft prove the plain rules engine is untouched, and the standard-chess cases (castling, en passant, promotion) switch it off deliberately since en passant cannot arise under the twist.

The pawn: what was actually wrong

Traced the exact sequence before changing anything, having already misread him once. Two findings:

  • The pawn's move options were already right. After a push and two twists the pawn on f4 could only play f5, and the move marker rendered exactly one square directly above it (dx 0, dy −82.9 px).
  • The carry was wrong. e2→e4 became f4, then f3 — sideways, then behind where it started. That is what "left or right or back" described.

So pawns are now frozen (D-009): a pawn holds its square and the pieces cycle among whichever of the four squares are not holding a pawn. Still a bijection, so a twist still cannot capture. It also deleted a rule — a frozen pawn can never reach the last rank by being carried, so promotion-by-twist is gone.

After: pawn pushed to e3, four twists later still on e3, only move e4 forward.

A harness flaw that could have invalidated every browser result

The browser suite insisted a pawn was being carried that the engine demonstrably did not carry — the same scenario passed in node. Chrome was serving cached JavaScript. Yesterday's fix to stop leaking a browser per run (reuse a live one) turned this from occasional into near-certain.

Fixed in the harness: create the target on about:blank, Network.enable + Network.setCacheDisabled, and only then Page.navigate. Disabling the cache after navigating is too late.

The tell was a node test and a browser test disagreeing about the same deterministic function. Suspect the harness before the code.

Four wrong assertions of mine, in a row

Writing the "no pawn is ever displaced" invariant took four goes, because a pawn legitimately changes square by being played, by being captured, and its path is legitimately blocked — and in the browser an unstubbed aiTurn was racing the scripted loop. Each failure looked like an engine bug and was not.

Where it ended

73 checks, 0 failures, and the first run guaranteed to be against current code. Search back to 586k nps after making the twist allocation-free (it had dropped to 385k when I added per-block arrays).

Two-player mode

Added hotseat as the first option of the existing Opponent select rather than a new control (D-011) — he had just removed a checkbox for being unnecessary. Choosing it hides You play, which needed a CSS fix: .row sets display: flex and beats the user agent's [hidden] rule, so setting hidden did nothing. The test asserts the computed display, not the attribute, because hidden === true passes while the element is still visible.

The nine scattered game.turn === playerColor comparisons all became one humanPlays() predicate, so the search cannot run in hotseat structurally rather than by remembering a guard in each branch.

No auto-flip between turns: the board already turns a quarter every move, and a 180° flip on top would be disorienting. Flip stays manual.

A bad assertion of my own, again

The self-play test asserted plies > 20 as a stand-in for "not deadlocked", and failed on a 12-ply checkmate — a good result, not a deadlock. Rewritten to run three games and require a legitimate outcome with no early draw: checkmate@57, checkmate@52, checkmate@35.

Slider out, and a real animation bug

Two more from Luqman. The Fold slider is gone (D-012) — the fold animation stays, only the manual control went.

The second was a genuine bug of mine, and he described it precisely: "the piece rotate with the board and then go back to its initial place." The sweep rotated every piece 90° about its tile centre. Correct while the twist was a plain quarter turn; wrong the moment pawns were frozen, because the pieces then cycle among only the free squares and a destination can be a quarter, a half or three quarters round — a pawn's is zero. So pieces arrived in the wrong place and jumped to the right one at the end, and a frozen pawn swung out and snapped straight back.

Now each piece sweeps by the actual angle between the square it came from and the square it is on (D-013). Both are cell centres of the same tile, so a pure rotation lands exactly.

Why no test caught it: every existing test checked board state or the paint angle, never where a piece was drawn. Pulled the maths into piecePosition(sq, now) and the suite now samples it at the start, middle and end of a sweep. Also crafted a position whose free squares are diagonally opposite, so the sweep must be 180° — that case fails instantly against a hard-coded 90°.

Third pass on the same sentence — the carry is uniform

Luqman: "the pieces should follow the rotation and stay. for example initial pieces location is a4, then the board rotate to the right, the pieces should now be at b4."

That concrete before/after settled what two rounds of prose could not. a4 is the top-left cell of the a3-b4 block and the plain quarter turn sends it to b4 — so freezing pawns (D-009) was the wrong fix, and worse, it made the carry unpredictable: the cycle had to skip occupied squares, so a piece on a4 with a pawn on b4 was shunted diagonally to b3 instead of turning to b4.

Reversed to the plain quarter turn for everything (D-014). Promotion-by-carry came back with it; the free-set machinery, its scratch buffers and blockBase went. Search went 586k → 803k nps, the plain 4-cycle being four writes instead of a scan plus a rotation.

His pawn rule survives, the right way round: a pawn only ever moves forward, wherever the board carries it. That was always true of the engine, and is now asserted for every pawn move in every position across 160 plies, so it cannot regress quietly. The board carrying a pawn is not the pawn moving — that distinction is the whole of it, and I should have separated the two on the first pass.

The lesson: all three passes cost the same mistake — treating a reported symptom as a specified rule. A concrete before/after is checkable in one line and leaves nothing to interpret. Worth asking for one early when a rule is in doubt, instead of picking a reading and building on it.

2026-09-13

The correction

Luqman: "i think u misunderstand me." He did not want the board to rotate as a flourish. He wanted a game mechanic: 2×2 blocks turning a quarter after a turn, carrying the pieces, so the position goes abnormal — and automatic, not the manual Fold slider.

Yesterday's whole-table spin (D-005) was the wrong thing. Removed rather than left switched off, so it could not fight the real mechanic.

One question worth asking

Which block turns? The answer — all of them — settled the architecture, not just the rule. "All blocks" is deterministic, so the twist went inside the engine's own make/unmake. Move generation, check, checkmate and the entire search then see the variant for free, and the AI plays it properly instead of playing normal chess into a scrambling board.

Worth noting the questioning went badly first: I offered three options for which block, when the answer was a fourth thing entirely. Asking earlier and more plainly would have got there quicker.

Reported before building

Turning every block maps the checkerboard onto its own colour inverse, so the board stays perfectly regular with light and dark swapped (D-008). Luqman's stated goal was an abnormal-looking board; that part is impossible with all sixteen turning, and the disorder lands entirely in the pieces. Said so up front rather than shipping and letting him notice.

The rule that had to change

First attempt was the principled one: your move must leave your king safe after the twist, enforced free by the existing legality test. It deadlocked — drew by stalemate on move 3. The permutation does not depend on your move, so a king boxed in by its own pieces is carried onto the same square every time, and if that square is covered every move is illegal. Dumped the position instead of assuming a bug:

8 r n b . k b n R      White to move, not in check, zero legal moves.
7 p p p p p p p p      King on e1, boxed in by its own pieces.
4 . . . q . . P .      e1 always carries to e2.
1 R N B Q K B N .      Black queen d4 always carries to d3, which covers e2.

So the twist yields instead of the player (D-007): it does not turn on a turn where it would expose your own king. Normal chess legality is then exactly untouched, which is asserted against a twist-free clone across 160 positions — that invariant is the thing that guarantees no freeze. It stands down on about one turn in seven.

A latent crash the variant exposed

if (inCheck) depth++ — the standard check extension — has no ceiling. In plain chess it terminates because you cannot stay in check forever. Under the twist kings are carried about constantly, check recurs, depth never falls and the search ran until the stack died. The bug was always there; the variant made it reachable. Now capped three ways: absolute ply, quiescence depth, and extension slack past the root depth.

Tests that caught my own mistakes

  • Two assertions failed while printing the right answer, because they raced the AI's reply. Fixed by measuring settled state, tying the paint angle to the engine's own record of which turns twisted, and stubbing aiTurn (a writable global in a classic script) for the one case that had to be isolated.
  • A "mid-twist" screenshot came back showing a settled board: Runtime.evaluate awaits promises, and twistOnce resolves on completion. void it.
  • An early assertion assumed the twist would make fewer moves legal. It makes more at first — a twist can rescue a king from check too. Wrong assumption, right code.

Where it ended

17 engine tests, 11 browser tests, plus the untouched 26 perft and 8 search. Self-play runs 85 plies and ends in checkmate. The twist gave check on its own in a real round (e4* Bd5+*).

A leak that looked like a slow test

The browser suite hung for minutes with no output. Cause: test/cdp.js spawned a headless Chrome per run and never closed it, and after a dozen runs the orphans wedged the debugging port. Now launch() reuses a live browser, each session closes its own tab, and run.sh reaps the browser at the end. Worth remembering that a leak in a harness presents as a slow or flaky test somewhere else.

  • Search reaches depth 4 with the twist vs 6 without (800k nps), because make now does 128 extra array writes.
  • Still not committed.
2026-09-12

What came in

Luqman sent IMG_3787.MP4, a 21-second vertical video, and said "make this chess game". ffmpeg was not installed, so frames came out via a short Swift + AVFoundation script — one per second — enough to identify the object: Auxetic Chess by Ruven Bals, reposted by viper_chess.

The fork

"Make this chess game" could mean a printable model or a playable game. Asked; Luqman chose the digital game (D-001).

Order of work

  1. Derived the mechanism first, before any rendering. d = a·√2·cos(45°+θ), checked numerically — worst hinge gap ~1e-15 of the tile edge.
  2. Rules engine, then perft. 26/26 published reference counts.
  3. Search — negamax, alpha-beta, quiescence, MVV-LVA, killers, tapered eval.
  4. Renderer, then artwork.
  5. Browser tests via a hand-rolled CDP client, so the artwork could be looked at rather than assumed.

Bugs found by actually looking

  • source-atop composites canvas-wide, so the piece highlight smeared bright columns across the whole board. Fixed by baking pieces into offscreen sprites.
  • lathePath walked the profile in the wrong order, self-intersecting the path; the stroke then drew a spurious diagonal across five of the six piece types. The knight was clean, which is what identified it.
  • 4 fps. ctx.filter = blur() per tile per frame. Baking the tile body, pin, shadow and backdrop into sprites took it to 54 fps.
  • A setTimeout-ed AI turn from a finished game fired into a new one and moved for the player. Now guarded by an epoch counter.
  • Three tactics tests "failed" that were my own bad positions — one asked for a queen move that does not exist. Rewrote the suite to derive mates from the proven generator instead of from my analysis.

Where it ended

Feature complete and tested: 26 perft + 8 search + 9 browser tests, all passing. Not committed — left for Luqman. Portfolio card added.

Later the same day — the table turns

Luqman asked for the board to rotate 90° after each move. Implemented as a transform on the way to the screen, with the click path inverted through it (D-005). Three things that were not obvious up front:

  • A rotating square's bounding box grows to 1.41× at 45°, so the corners clipped until the scale backed off mid-turn.
  • There was a 190 ms window after each move — the pause letting the piece land — where the board looked settled and input re-opened. Closed by baking a start delay into the tween instead of sleeping before creating it.
  • The search blocks the thread, so the turn has to finish before the engine starts or the rotation freezes halfway.

The spin suite is 8/8, and the earlier suites still pass once the rules tests turn the spin off — they are about chess, not the table.

What proves it works, from each file's own header comment

Tests and tools

Test files

Everything in test/. `test/run.sh` runs the Node suites first, then serves the folder and runs the browser suites in order. A dash means the file opens with code rather than a comment.

FileWhat it does
test/run.shFull test suite. The browser tests need Chrome and a local server.
test/ai_test.js—
test/cdp.jsMinimal Chrome DevTools Protocol driver. No dependencies.
test/gameplay.js—
test/geom_check.jsRotating-squares auxetic mechanism. 4x4 grid of rigid square tiles, side a, hinged at shared corners. Tile (i,j) rotates by stheta where s = +1 on "even" tiles, -1 on odd. Claim: the mechanism stays closed iff centre pitch d = asqrt(2)*cos(45deg + theta). Verify numerically that every shared corner of every neighbour pair coincides.
test/hotseat.jsTwo-player mode, driven through the real UI: both sides accept clicks, the computer never moves, and one undo takes back one turn.
test/leaderboard_browser.jsThe start screen and the shared leaderboard, through the real page. The live leaderboard is never touched: the page's leaderboard is swapped for a stand-in server that keeps its data in memory but follows the real rules -- names claimed by PIN, five wrong PINs lock a name, a win is saved only if server/replay.js confirms it, and the same game counts once. The winning game itself is a real one, played by the engine in node.
test/leaderboard_test.jsThe leaderboard client on its own, with a fake network: what it asks for, what it sends, and how it reports trouble. Nothing here touches the internet.
test/online_live.jsThe real, deployed leaderboard, tested from outside the way a stranger would see it. Not part of run.sh: it needs the internet and a deployed project. node test/online_live.js It uses throwaway names starting "zz-live-" and deletes them at the end (through the management API, with SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN from ~/.claude/.env), so the public board is left as it was.
test/perft.js—
test/repeatable.jsMakes an engine test give the same answer on every run. Two things used to make results differ from run to run: 1. Chance. The tests play random games, and the casual and club levels pick at random among near-best moves (ai.js, jitter). seed(n) replaces Math.random with a fixed sequence, so every run plays the same games and the engine makes the same picks. 2. The clock. think searches deeper until its time budget runs out, so a busy machine searches less deeply and can choose a different move. fullDepth(fn) stops the clock while fn runs, so every search goes to its level's full depth however loaded the machine is. Use it where a test checks which move the engine picks; leave it off where a test is about speed. The engine files are loaded with new Function, which shares this process's Math and Date, so both reach inside the engine without changing it.
test/replay_test.jsThe server's check on a claimed win: a real finished game is accepted, and every way of faking or bending one is refused.
test/stop_browser.jsStop turning, played through the real UI: the button, the two stopped moves, the count, undo, and the computer respecting a stop.
test/stop_test.jsStop turning: a player may stop the board for their move and the reply. Run with node from the project root.
test/twist_browser.jsThe twist, driven through the real UI: does a click actually carry the pieces round, does the animation land, and does undo put everything back.
test/twist_test.jsThe twist: every 2x2 block turns a quarter after each move, carrying pieces. Run with node from the project root.

Game source

The six scripts index.html loads, in the order they load.

FileWhat it does
js/chess.jsChess rules engine. 0x88 board representation. A square index is rank*16 + file; a square is off-board iff (sq & 0x88) != 0, which makes every "did I walk off the edge" test a single mask.
js/ai.jsSearch: negamax with alpha-beta, iterative deepening, quiescence, MVV-LVA capture ordering and killer moves. Runs synchronously inside a time budget so it works from file:// with no worker.
js/pieces.jsPiece artwork. Each piece is drawn once into an offscreen sprite and then blitted, which caches the work and -- importantly -- keeps the source-atop sheen scoped to the piece instead of smearing it across the whole board. Sprite space is a 120x120 unit box with 10 units of padding, wrapping the 100x100 box the shapes below are authored in: y down, standing on y = 92.
js/leaderboard.jsThe shared leaderboard: one table of wins per computer level, online. Reading is a plain request to the standings table with Supabase's public key. Writing never happens from here: a name check or a win goes to the leaderboard server function, which checks the PIN and replays the game before anything is saved (supabase/functions/leaderboard, server/replay.js). Nothing here touches the page, and fetch can be swapped for a fake, so the node tests exercise it without a network. Every method throws when the leaderboard cannot be reached; the page treats that as "offline" and the game carries on unranked. This file is also bundled into the server function, for cleanName, so the server cleans a name exactly the way the start screen does.
js/board.jsAuxetic board renderer, on Phaser. The board is 16 rigid square tiles, side a, each carrying a 2x2 patch of the checkerboard. Tiles are hinged at shared corners and alternate their rotation +theta / -theta. For the hinges to stay joined the centre pitch must be d = a * sqrt(2) * cos(45deg + theta) theta = 0deg -> d = a tiles flush, solid 8x8 board (playable) theta = -45deg -> d = asqrt2 fully bloomed, exactly 2x the area Because every tile carries the same 2x2 patch -- square (f,r) has colour parity (f+r)%2, and a tile starts at even f and even r, so its local parity is (u+v)%2 regardless of which tile it is -- all 16 tiles are identical. That is why the real thing can be printed 16 times from one model. --- All of the geometry above is unchanged and still computed here by hand; what Phaser replaced is everything *underneath it. The tiles, pins, pieces and backdrop used to be blitted with ctx.drawImage sixty times a second. They are now Phaser game objects on a WebGL renderer, which is what buys the rest: real tweens, a particle system, camera shake, per-object filters, and a sound manager that can overlap samples. Two rules kept the swap safe: 1. BoardView exposes exactly the API js/main.js and the six browser tests already used -- squareLayout, pointToSquare, isSolid, animateTo, twistOnce, setThetaManual, setTwistAngle, animateMove, flipped, selected, legalTargets, lastMove, checkSquare, pieceAnim, hover, onSquareClick -- with the same units: CSS pixels measured from the canvas's top-left. 2. The animation state machine still runs on its own clock, in step(), not on Phaser tweens. The fold and the twist have to resolve their promises at the exact moment the engine expects, and isSolid gates input for the whole transition. Phaser's tweens drive the decoration instead.
js/main.jsGame wiring: input, the AI turn, the move list, and the fold.
